difficultyRationale: Requires comparing the cost profile of a heap against a fully sorted array across both insertion and extraction, not just one operation in isolation.
prompt: A backend task scheduler must always process the task with the highest priority next, while new tasks are continuously added. Compared to maintaining a fully sorted array of tasks, what is the main advantage of using a binary heap-backed priority queue?
explanation: A binary heap keeps only a partial order (the heap property) rather than a full sort, which lets both inserting a new task and extracting the highest-priority task run in O(log n). Keeping a full array sorted after every insertion costs O(n) per insertion, because an element may need to be shifted into its correct sorted position among all existing elements.

options.text: A heap gives O(1) extraction and O(1) insertion, which is strictly better than any array-based approach in every case.
options.explanation: A binary heap's insert and extract-highest-priority operations are both O(log n), not O(1); claiming O(1) for both overstates the heap's actual complexity.

options.text: A heap keeps all elements in fully sorted order at all times, just like a sorted array, but can update that order in O(log n) by storing the complete binary tree compactly in a single backing array and adjusting parent-child index relationships.
options.explanation: A heap only guarantees the heap property (each parent has higher priority than its children), not a full total order across all elements; reading elements in sorted order from a heap is not O(log n) per element overall.

options.text: A heap avoids the need for comparisons between tasks entirely by using hashing to determine priority order.
options.explanation: Heaps are fundamentally comparison-based (or key-based) structures; they rely on comparing priorities to decide placement, and do not use hashing to determine ordering at all.

options.text: A heap supports inserting a task and extracting the highest-priority task in O(log n) each, while keeping an array fully sorted after every insertion costs O(n) per insertion.
options.explanation: Correct: the heap only restores a weaker partial order after each change (sift-up/sift-down along one path of height log n), whereas keeping an array fully sorted after every insertion needs the new element shifted into place among all existing elements.
